steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on mapping the X3D 3D CNN for human action recognition onto FPGAs. Explain why 3D CNNs matter for video, why they are expensive and why FPGAs are a good fit, how our work differs from earlier FPGA work, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- From 2D CNNs to 3D CNNs for video
- 3D CNNs in human action recognition
- Computational cost and FPGAs as accelerators
- This work: FPGA architecture for X3D
- Adapting to devices/constraints; contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- 2D to 3D CNNs
  - 2D CNNs excel at image tasks
  - video tasks growing: surveillance, autonomous driving, elderly/patient monitoring -> need temporal domain
  - 3D CNNs frequently used for video and volumetric data
  - extra dimension (time or depth) -> features of added dimension, better learning capacity
- HAR
  - exceptional performance in human action recognition
  - motion across frames, no dedicated time-domain techniques (e.g., LSTMs)
  - Figure 1: 3D CNNs dominate pareto front on Kinetics-400 (cite)
  - vision transformers reaching pareto front too, but orders of magnitude more GFLOPs
- Cost and FPGAs
  - extra dimension -> bigger workloads, compute and memory vs 2D
  - GPUs, FPGAs, ASICs used for acceleration
  - FPGAs: more flexible than ASICs, more energy efficient than GPUs
  - fast-evolving 3D CNN designs -> need quickly adaptable platform
- This work
  - prior FPGA work: C3D and R(2+1)D, below pareto front on Kinetics
  - here: X3D (cite), pareto front of accuracy vs number of parameters (Figure 1)
  - automated optimization, SDF graph transformations; streaming architecture + Synchronous Data Flow (SDF) (cite); target FPGA requirements
- Adaptation and contributions
  - target platform/resource constraints change with application
  - Figure 2: adapts to devices and utilisation limits, pareto front solutions
  - extend SDF graph model to irregular blocks with branching
  - automate/optimise X3D mapping to different FPGAs given resources and memory bandwidth
  - two streaming optimizations: prior batch statistics for GAP layers; 16-bit fixed-point quantization of weights and feature maps

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Two-dimensional CNNs have done very well on image-related tasks in recent years. But more focus and more applications now come from video-related tasks, like video surveillance, autonomous driving, and elderly/patient monitoring, and these have made it necessary to develop algorithms that include and account for the temporal domain. Three-dimensional CNNs are one of the techniques used most often for video and volumetric data. 3D CNNs add an extra dimension, like time or depth, compared to 2D CNNs, and so they improve their learning capacity because they also extract features that are relevant to the newly added dimension of the input.

3D CNNs have shown exceptional performance especially in human action recognition. With 3D CNNs, human motion across the frames of a video can be interpreted, so many different human actions can be detected without dedicated time-domain techniques (e.g., LSTMs). Figure 1 shows that 3D CNNs dominate the pareto front in one of the most widely used HAR benchmarks, Kinetics-400. Vision transformers have recently also started to push some designs to the pareto front, but these networks need orders of magnitude more GFLOPs to run.

3D CNNs can capture time- or depth-related features, but the additional input dimension often leads to bigger workloads and higher computational and memory requirements than 2D CNNs. Many hardware devices, like GPUs, FPGAs and ASICs, have been used to deal with the high processing requirements of 3D CNNs and to give high performing systems. FPGAs are an attractive acceleration platform because they are more flexible than ASICs and more energy efficient than GPUs. Also, 3D CNN model designs change quickly, so a platform is needed that can adapt fast to the requirements of any new model.

- This work
  - earlier FPGA acceleration: C3D and R(2+1)D, not on pareto front in Kinetics
  - X3D (cite), pareto front of accuracy vs. parameters (Figure 1)
  - automated optimization, SDF graph transformations, streaming architecture, Synchronous Data Flow (SDF) (cite), target FPGA requirements
- Adaptation and contributions
  - constraints vary by application; Figure 2 shows adaptation to devices and utilisation limits
  - SDF extension for irregular blocks with branching
  - automated, optimised X3D mapping for different FPGAs (resources, memory bandwidth)
  - prior batch statistics for GAP layers; 16-bit fixed-point quantization

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Two-dimensional CNNs have done very well on image-related tasks in recent years. But more focus and more applications now come from video-related tasks, like video surveillance, autonomous driving, and elderly/patient monitoring, and these have made it necessary to develop algorithms that include and account for the temporal domain. Three-dimensional CNNs are one of the techniques used most often for video and volumetric data. 3D CNNs add an extra dimension, like time or depth, compared to 2D CNNs, and so they improve their learning capacity because they also extract features that are relevant to the newly added dimension of the input.

3D CNNs have shown exceptional performance especially in human action recognition. With 3D CNNs, human motion across the frames of a video can be interpreted, so many different human actions can be detected without dedicated time-domain techniques (e.g., LSTMs). Figure 1 shows that 3D CNNs dominate the pareto front in one of the most widely used HAR benchmarks, Kinetics-400. Vision transformers have recently also started to push some designs to the pareto front, but these networks need orders of magnitude more GFLOPs to run.

3D CNNs can capture time- or depth-related features, but the additional input dimension often leads to bigger workloads and higher computational and memory requirements than 2D CNNs. Many hardware devices, like GPUs, FPGAs and ASICs, have been used to deal with the high processing requirements of 3D CNNs and to give high performing systems. FPGAs are an attractive acceleration platform because they are more flexible than ASICs and more energy efficient than GPUs. Also, 3D CNN model designs change quickly, so a platform is needed that can adapt fast to the requirements of any new model.

Previous FPGA-based acceleration of 3D CNN models focused on C3D and R(2+1)D, and their performance is below the pareto front in recent benchmarks like Kinetics. This work instead proposes an FPGA architecture for X3D, which is a 3D CNN model on the pareto front of accuracy vs. number of parameters, as Figure 1 shows. We explore the design space of X3D with an automated optimization approach and by applying transformations to the SDF graph, based on a streaming architecture and the Synchronous Data Flow (SDF) computation model, and taking into account the requirements of the target FPGA platform.

The target FPGA platform or the resource constraints may change depending on the application or system requirements. Figure 2 shows that the proposed hardware design can adapt to different devices and to different restrictions on the FPGA utilisation percentage, and gives pareto front solutions in each case. The key contributions of this paper are:

- We extend the SDF graph model, which is used to capture the performance requirements when mapping CNNs to streaming architectures, so that it explicitly handles irregular blocks with branching, which are used a lot in modern CNN models.
- We automate and optimise the mapping of the X3D model, a state of the art model for Human Action Recognition, to different FPGA devices, taking into account the FPGA resources available and the memory bandwidth characteristics.
- Two streaming-centric optimizations that improve the dataflow characteristics of the X3D network: using prior batch statistics for GAP layers, and quantizing the model weights and feature maps to 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, two-dimensional CNNs have excelled at image-related tasks. The growing focus on, and number of applications arising from, video-related tasks such as video surveillance, autonomous driving, and elderly/patient monitoring have made it necessary to develop algorithms that include and account for the temporal domain. Three-dimensional CNNs are one of the most frequently applied techniques for dealing with video and volumetric data. By adding an extra dimension, such as time or depth, over 2D CNNs, 3D CNNs improve their learning capacity by also extracting features relevant to the newly added dimension of the input.

3D CNNs have demonstrated exceptional performance especially in the task of human action recognition. They enable the interpretation of human motion across the frames of a video, allowing a variety of human actions to be detected without dedicated time-domain techniques (e.g., LSTMs). As Figure 1 shows, 3D CNNs dominate the pareto front in one of the most widely used HAR benchmarks, Kinetics-400 [1], while the recent emergence of vision transformers has also begun to drive some designs to the pareto front; however, such networks require orders of magnitude more GFLOPs to operate.

While 3D CNNs are capable of capturing time- or depth-related features, the additional input dimension frequently results in greater workloads and computational and memory requirements compared to 2D CNNs. Numerous hardware devices, including GPUs, FPGAs, and ASICs, have been used to mitigate the high processing requirements of 3D CNNs and provide high performing systems. FPGAs are an attractive candidate acceleration platform, since they offer greater flexibility than ASICs and are more energy efficient than GPUs. Furthermore, the rapid evolution of 3D CNN model designs calls for a platform that can quickly adapt to new model requirements.

Previous FPGA-based acceleration of 3D CNN models focused on C3D and R(2+1)D, whose performance falls short of the pareto front in recent benchmarks such as Kinetics. In contrast, this work proposes an FPGA architecture for X3D [2], a 3D CNN model lying on the pareto front of accuracy vs. number of parameters, as shown in Figure 1. Using an automated optimization approach and applying transformations to the SDF graph, we explore the design space of X3D based on a streaming architecture and the Synchronous Data Flow (SDF) [3] computation model, taking into account the requirements of the target FPGA platform.

The target FPGA platform or resource constraints may change depending on the application or system requirements. As Figure 2 shows, the proposed hardware design can adapt to different devices as well as to varied restrictions on the FPGA utilisation percentage, resulting in pareto front solutions in each circumstance. The key contributions of this paper are the following:

- The extension of the SDF graph model used for capturing the performance requirements in CNN mapping to streaming architectures, to explicitly address irregular blocks with branching, which are widely used in modern CNN models.
- The automation and optimisation of the mapping of the X3D model, a state of the art model for Human Action Recognition, to different FPGA devices, taking into account the available FPGA resources and memory bandwidth characteristics.
- Two streaming-centric optimizations to improve the dataflow characteristics of the X3D network: the use of prior batch statistics for GAP layers, and the quantization of the model weights and feature maps to 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic.

References:
[1] Kay, W., Carreira, J., Simonyan, K., Zhang, B., Hillier, C., Vijayanarasimhan, S., Viola, F., Green, T., Back, T., Natsev, P., Suleyman, M., and Zisserman, A. The Kinetics Human Action Video Dataset. Tech. rep., 5 2017.
[2] Feichtenhofer, C. X3D: Expanding Architectures for Efficient Video Recognition. In IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) (2020), Feichtenhofer Christoph, Ed., pp. 200–210.
[3] Lee, E. A., and Messerschmitt, D. G. Synchronous data flow. In Proceedings of the IEEE (1987), vol. 75, pp. 1235–1245.
